newsitem.title: USA: Coffee drinkers may be in for higher prices.
newsitem.headline: Coffee drinkers may be in for higher prices.

text.p: Coffee drinkers can expect higher prices this year amid depleted stocks at roasters and an expected smaller crop next season in Brazil, the world's largest producer, market analysts said Friday.

Tight supplies due to a long dockworkers' strike in in Colombia and the outlook for lower harvests elsewhere in the coming year have already pushed futures prices sharply higher in recent weeks, to their highest level since September, 1995.
No U.S. coffee roaster has raised its posted prices yet, but analysts say increases may not be far off if the trend in the futures market continues.

"If the market keeps rallying, roasters might change their minds," said Merrill Lynch analyst Judith Ganes. "Roasters may have to raise prices in the future but not right now. They do not want to jolt consumers."
While U.S. coffee processors have no immediate plans to hike retail prices, they said they will continue to closely watch futures on the Coffee, Sugar and Cocoa exchange.

"Like everyone else, we watch the market to see if there is a sustainable price," said a spokeswoman for Folgers Coffee Co., a unit of Proctor and Gamble. "Right now we do not have news of a (retail) price increase."
Earlier this week, however, Procter and Gamble's Canadian division said it will raise the price of Folgers coffee in Canada on Feb. 1 to reflect gains in green bean prices.

"Our intention is to reflect North American green bean prices," said a spokeswoman for Proctor's Canadian unit. "We last lowered the price on Aug. 1, and that was to be in line with competitive pricing."

Coffee industry analysts said a prolonged rise in coffee bean prices will eventually feed through to higher prices on the supermarket shelves. Based on the supply outlook, prices look set to go higher, they added.
Dwindling coffee inventories are at the root of the sudden surge in prices on the futures market. Physical stocks of coffee in both producing and consuming countries have fallen sharply.
"Total supplies have not been this tight in 20 years," Ganes said.
Still, traders said the tightness of current supplies may have caught many roasters by surprise.

Normally, an increased flow of newly harvested, high quality "arabica" coffee starts arriving from Latin America during the first quarter of the year. But aggressive buying by European roasters has absorbed more new crop than usual from Mexico, Nicaragua and other Central American producers.

Analysts said chances of a price rise by top U.S. roasters also will hinge on the size of next year's crop in Brazil. Brazil produces about one-quarter of the world's total coffee supply annually, harvested from July onward.
"It depends on inventory levels and it depends in part on the Brazil crop," Prudential securities analyst Arthur Stevenson said. "This is a very uncertain situation."

Preliminary forecasts by the Brazilian government have pegged the country's coming 1997/98 coffee crop between 18 million and 20 million bags compared with an estimated 25 million bags a year earlier. Each bag weighs 132 pounds.
A sharp drop in Brazil's production two years ago due to two devastating frosts sent coffee prices soaring to the highest levels in nearly a decade.

At that time, coffe roasters were quick to raise their prices to keep pace with skyrocketing futures prices. But some analysts said the higher prices may have prompted consumers to cut back on the amount of coffee they drink.
This time around, roasters may be more wary of hiking prices too quickly and scaring consumers away, analysts said.
On Friday, March delivery coffee at New York's Coffee, Sugar and Cocoa Exchange closed down 3.15 cents per pound to $136.90, but was still up 33 percent from its closing price on Dec. 6.
